analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board to identify excessive prescription drug prices and revoke patents when makers refuse to cut them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 1996, sent to the House Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a five-member Prescription Drug Price Review Board, staffed by experts with no recent drug-industry ties, to review the price of every prescription drug. The board would decide whether prices or price increases were excessive, using factors like manufacturing costs, prices in other countries, and how much of a drug's research the federal government paid for. If a manufacturer refused to bring an excessive price down after a public hearing, the board could revoke the drug's patent, opening it to generic competition. The bill also required an annual, plain-language consumer guide to drug prices and directed a study of drug pricing and affordability.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay for prescription drugs, including seniors and uninsured households, who would gain a government check on drug prices, public information about which drugs are overpriced, and the threat of generic competition when prices stay excessive.

how_it_helps.text: The board would review the price of every prescription drug and publish its findings and methods for consumers and health care providers.
If a price was found excessive and the manufacturer would not reduce it, the board could revoke the drug's patent, allowing cheaper generic versions.
Board members could not have worked in pharmaceutical manufacturing during the previous three years, and the board would publish an annually updated consumer's guide to prescription drug prices.
The bill required a study of why many Americans struggle to afford prescription drugs and of options for making drugs available to all who need them, including Medicare negotiation.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose prices would face review and whose patents could be revoked for refusing to cut excessive prices, plus taxpayers who would fund the new board and its staff.

drawbacks.text: Revoking a patent as a price-control penalty is a blunt remedy; critics argue that weakening patent protection reduces the financial incentive to develop new drugs, and the bill itself directed a study of whether patent terms should be adjusted so makers could still recoup research costs.

The bill created a new federal agency with subpoena power and mandatory price reviews of every drug on the market, which supporters of a lighter regulatory touch would view as costly government overreach into drug pricing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing high drug prices, the potential benefits were substantial: direct price review, public pricing information, and a credible penalty backed by patent revocation. The main cost fell on drug makers, not consumers, though an honest reading has to weigh the risk that aggressive price controls and patent revocation could discourage investment in new medicines. The bill offered no offsetting research incentives beyond directing a study of the question.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, then to its health subcommittee a week later, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Johnson of South Dakota introduced the Prescription Drug Consumer Protection Act of 1996 on June 20, 1996, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Commerce on June 20, 1996.
On June 28, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where no further action was taken.
No committee or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off, since their pricing faced no review and their patents faced no revocation risk; consumers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (Subcommittee on Health and Environment)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the health subcommittee, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the remainder of the 104th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Commerce Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would subject every drug price to federal review, require disclosure of costs and pricing, and revoke patents when prices were not reduced, directly threatening the industry's pricing power and patent-protected revenue. Consumers bear the cost of unreviewed prices, so the industry's interest in defeating oversight ran against the public's.
